It now placed my altitude at 132,000 feet, or twenty-five miles, which meant that I could survey no less than one three-hundred-and-twentieth of the earth’s total surface. By nine o’clock the land to the east had vanished again, though before losing it I noticed that the balloon was drifting quickly north-northwest. The curvature of the ocean beneath me was unmistakable, despite the clouds moving back and forth across my view. I now observed that even the faintest wisps of vapour never rose higher than ten miles above sea level.

“At half past nine I experimented by releasing a handful of feathers through the valve. Instead of floating as I expected, they fell straight down together, like a bullet, at tremendous speed. Within a few seconds they had disappeared. At first I could make no sense of this extraordinary sight: I could hardly believe that my upward speed had suddenly increased so enormously. Then I realised that the air had become too thin to support even feathers. They really were falling as rapidly as they appeared, and what had startled me was the combined effect of their downward movement and my own ascent.

“By ten o’clock I had very little that required immediate attention. Everything was proceeding beautifully, and I believed the balloon was climbing faster with every moment, although I no longer had a way to measure the rate of acceleration. I felt neither pain nor discomfort of any kind. My spirits were better than at any time since leaving Rotterdam. I occupied myself by checking my various pieces of equipment and renewing the air inside the chamber. I decided to refresh it regularly every forty minutes, chiefly to safeguard my health, rather than because such frequent renewal was strictly necessary. Meanwhile, I could not resist imagining what lay ahead. My fancy delighted in the wild and dreamlike landscapes of the moon. For once free of restraint, my imagination wandered wherever it pleased through the endlessly changing marvels of a shadowy, shifting country. At one moment I saw ancient, venerable forests, jagged cliffs, and waterfalls crashing thunderously into bottomless chasms. Then, abruptly, I found myself in the stillness of deserted places at noon, where no breath of wind ever entered. Immense meadows of poppies and slender flowers resembling lilies stretched into an exhausting distance, everything forever silent and motionless.

This was the housekeeper, Mrs. Umney, whom Mrs. Otis had agreed, at Lady Canterville’s urgent entreaty, to retain in her old employment. As they stepped down she gave each a deep curtsey, saying in a quaintly old-fashioned fashion, ‘I welcome you to Canterville Chase.’ They followed her through the handsome Tudor hall and into the library, a long, low apartment lined with black oak, with a great stained-glass window at its farther end. Tea awaited them there. Having removed their wraps, they seated themselves and surveyed the room while Mrs. Umney served them.

Mrs. Otis suddenly noticed a dull crimson mark on the floor beside the hearth. Entirely unaware of its true significance, she remarked to Mrs. Umney, ‘I fear something has been spilled there.’

‘Yes, madam,’ the elderly housekeeper answered softly, ‘blood was spilled upon that spot.’

‘How dreadful!’ exclaimed Mrs. Otis. ‘Bloodstains in a sitting room are quite disagreeable to me. Have it taken away immediately.’

The old woman smiled, replying in the same hushed, mysterious tones, ‘That is Lady Eleanore de Canterville’s blood. Her own husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, murdered her on that very spot in 1575. He lived nine years after her death, then suddenly vanished under most mysterious circumstances. His body has never come to light, yet his guilty ghost continues to haunt the Chase. Tourists and other visitors have greatly admired this bloodstain, which cannot be removed.’

‘Complete nonsense,’ Washington Otis declared. ‘Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will get rid of it in a moment.’ Before the terrified housekeeper could prevent him, he was on his knees, briskly rubbing the floor with a little stick resembling a black cosmetic. Within moments not a trace of the stain remained.

‘I knew Pinkerton could manage it!’ he announced in triumph, glancing at his admiring relatives. Scarcely had he spoken when a dreadful lightning flash illuminated the gloomy chamber, and a tremendous thunderclap brought everyone to their feet. Mrs. Umney swooned.

‘What an outrageous climate!’ observed the American Minister placidly, lighting a long cheroot. ‘I suppose the old country is so crowded that there isn’t sufficient fine weather to go round. I have always thought emigration the only remedy for England.’

‘Hiram, my dear,’ cried Mrs. Otis, ‘how are we to manage a woman who faints?’

‘Bill her for it, as you would for breakages,’ the Minister replied. ‘That will put a stop to her fainting.’ And sure enough, in a few moments Mrs. Umney recovered.

Soul and body, body and soul—what mysteries they were! The soul contained animal instincts, while the body had its moments of spiritual awareness. The senses could elevate us, and the intellect could debase us. Who could determine where a physical impulse ended and a psychological one began? The arbitrary definitions offered by ordinary psychologists were so superficial. Yet choosing between the competing schools was so difficult. Was the soul a shadow dwelling in a house of sin? Or did the body actually exist within the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? The separation of spirit and matter was mysterious, and their union was equally so.

He began to ask himself whether psychology could ever become so exact a science that it would expose every tiny mechanism of life. As things stood, we consistently misunderstood ourselves and seldom understood anyone else. Experience had no moral worth. It was simply the label people attached to their mistakes. Moralists usually treated it as a warning, credited it with some power to improve character, and praised it for teaching us what to pursue and what to avoid. But experience had no power to move us. Like conscience itself, it scarcely caused us to act. What it really showed was only that our future would repeat our past, and that a sin we first committed with disgust would later be repeated many times with pleasure.

To him it was obvious that experiment provided the sole means of analysing the passions scientifically. Dorian Gray was certainly a subject perfectly suited to his purposes, promising abundant and fruitful discoveries. His sudden, reckless love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological phenomenon of considerable interest. Curiosity undoubtedly played a large part, together with his appetite for unfamiliar experiences. Still, this was a highly complicated passion, far from a simple one. Whatever purely sensual instincts of boyhood it contained had been reshaped by the imagination into something the boy himself thought entirely removed from the senses. For precisely that reason, it was all the more dangerous. The passions whose origins we concealed from ourselves exercised the strongest tyranny over us. Our weakest motives were those whose nature we recognised. Often, when we believed ourselves to be conducting experiments on other people, we were actually experimenting on ourselves.

As Lord Henry sat absorbed in these reflections, someone knocked at the door. His valet came in to remind him that it was time to change for dinner.
